Lessons.Title: Domain and Range (Part 1)
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: identify possible inputs (domain) and outputs (range) for a function by reading real-world restrictions, distinguishing discrete from continuous quantities and checking unreasonable values. First-party Edulytiks adaptation of Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition Unit 4 Lesson 10, https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/4/10/preparation.html and student lesson https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/students/1/4/10/index.html (CC BY 4.0). The source uses dog barks, square areas and event enrollment, including optional graphing technology.

Original fictional workshop revenue example: participation n must be a whole-number count between 5 and12 inclusive; price is $7 per student plus a $10 single sponsorship amount, so revenue R(n)=7n+10 dollars. Domain {5,6,7,8,9,10,11,12}, not the entire interval of real numbers. Range {45,52,59,66,73,80,87,94} dollars. R(8.5) can be computed arithmetically but is not an input in this scenario.

For a square's area A(s)=s² with physical side length s≥0 centimetres, domain is [0,∞) and range is [0,∞) square centimetres; if a non-degenerate actual square is required, both should exclude zero. The formula alone would permit any real s algebraically, but context disallows negative lengths. Distinguish domain of the formula from domain chosen for modeling.

Student task: sort proposed inputs and outputs for both functions, explain why 8.5 participants and negative lengths are impossible, state domain/range in lists or inequalities as appropriate, and critique an unsupported continuous graph in a discrete situation. Teacher-scored rubric 0–2 for correct variable/domain, correctly enumerated range, graph/context distinction and reasoning about boundary cases.

KeyConcepts.Title: Domain
KeyConcepts.Definition: The set of allowed input values of a function.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Combine algebraic definition and contextual restrictions.

KeyConcepts.Title: Range
KeyConcepts.Definition: The outputs produced by allowed inputs, not all algebraically possible numbers.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Evaluate the function at each permitted discrete input when finite.

KeyConcepts.Title: Discrete versus continuous
KeyConcepts.Definition: Counts are integers, while measured lengths may vary continuously.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Choose a graphical representation matching the domain.
KeyConcepts.Example: Enrollment uses isolated dots; physical length s≥0 uses a continuous ray.

WorkedExamples.Title: Find workshop domain
WorkedExamples.Question: The workshop accepts between 5 and12 people inclusive. Give domain.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the exact first-party function definition and independently verify each substitution, graph feature and domain.
Steps: Participants cannot be negative or fractional.
Include endpoints because the restrictions are inclusive.
WorkedExamples.Check: n=8.5 is not a physically allowed count.

WorkedExamples.Title: Find workshop revenue range
WorkedExamples.Question: Use R(n)=7n+10 on the specified domain.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the exact first-party function definition and independently verify each substitution, graph feature and domain.
Steps: Add $7 for every subsequent allowed whole-person increment.
No values between the listed totals occur in this discrete model.
WorkedExamples.Check: Eight allowed inputs produce eight distinct outputs.

WorkedExamples.Title: Classify square-area inputs
WorkedExamples.Question: Determine physical domain and range of A(s)=s².
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the exact first-party function definition and independently verify each substitution, graph feature and domain.
Steps: s represents side length in centimetres, so negative values are impossible.
Every nonnegative area a can be reached with s=sqrt(a).
If side length zero is allowed as a limiting case, both include zero.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Domain s≥0 cm, range A≥0 cm² under the zero-permitted model.
WorkedExamples.Check: The output of a length is squared, with square-centimetre units.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Writing every real n between 5 and12 for people

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Domain is inputs, range is attained outputs.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using negative side lengths because squaring yields positive area
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Algebraic output does not override geometry.

SummaryPoints: Domain and range depend on mathematical rule and intended context.
Discrete counting domains create discrete ranges.
R(n)=7n+10 over n5–12 has eight exact output values.
Teacher reviews justification and non-domain examples.
